slides.title: Network and Application Attacks
points: Recognize network and application attacks from traffic behavior, protocol abuse, replay, interception, code execution, or privilege changes.
Security+ Objective 2.4: given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.

slides.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS)
slides.teach: A denial-of-service attack launched from many systems to overwhelm a target.

course.learn: A denial-of-service attack launched from many systems to overwhelm a target.
course.example: Thousands of compromised hosts flood one website.
course.exam: Many systems flood one target → DDoS.
course.check_q: Which attack overwhelms a target from many systems?

slides.title: Amplified DDoS
slides.teach: A DDoS technique where small attacker requests trigger much larger responses toward the victim.

course.learn: A DDoS technique where small attacker requests trigger much larger responses toward the victim.
course.example: Small DNS requests generate large responses toward the victim.
course.check_q: Which DDoS technique multiplies traffic using larger responses?

slides.title: Reflected DDoS
slides.teach: A DDoS technique where attackers spoof the victim's address so third-party systems send responses to the victim.

course.learn: A DDoS technique where attackers spoof the victim's address so third-party systems send responses to the victim.

breakdown.explanation: Other systems are tricked into replying to the victim.

course.why: Reflection recruits third-party servers and obscures the attacker.
course.example: DNS servers send replies to a victim that never queried them.
course.exam: Third parties reply to victim → REFLECTED.
course.check_q: Which DDoS technique uses spoofed victim addresses?

slides.title: DNS Attack
slides.teach: An attack targeting DNS resolution, records, caches, or infrastructure.

course.learn: An attack targeting DNS resolution, records, caches, or infrastructure.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker manipulates or disrupts name resolution.

course.why: DNS attacks can redirect users or disrupt services.
course.example: A legitimate domain resolves to a malicious IP.

slides.title: Wireless Attack
slides.teach: An attack targeting Wi-Fi or other wireless communication.

course.learn: An attack targeting Wi-Fi or other wireless communication.

slides.title: On-path Attack
slides.teach: An attacker positions between communicating parties to intercept or alter traffic.

course.learn: An attacker positions between communicating parties to intercept or alter traffic.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker sits in the middle.

course.why: The attacker can steal or modify data in transit.
course.example: Login traffic is intercepted between user and server.
course.check_q: Which attack places the attacker between communicating parties?

slides.title: Credential Replay
slides.teach: Previously captured credentials or authentication material are reused to gain access.

course.learn: Previously captured credentials or authentication material are reused to gain access.

breakdown.explanation: Steal authentication material, then reuse it.

course.why: Some auth artifacts can be replayed without knowing the original secret.
course.example: A stolen authentication token is reused successfully.
course.check_q: Which attack reuses captured authentication material?

slides.title: Malicious Code
slides.teach: Attacker-supplied code executes in a target environment.

course.learn: Attacker-supplied code executes in a target environment.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker's code runs on the target.

course.why: Code execution can give direct control of system behavior.
course.example: Attacker-controlled code executes on a server.
course.check_q: Which indicator describes attacker-supplied code executing?

slides.title: Injection
slides.teach: Untrusted input is interpreted as commands or code by an application.

course.learn: Untrusted input is interpreted as commands or code by an application.
course.why: Unsafe input handling can alter commands or queries.
course.example: A form field is interpreted as a backend command.
course.check_q: Which application attack turns untrusted input into commands?

slides.title: Buffer Overflow
slides.teach: Too much data is written to memory, potentially overwriting control data.

course.learn: Too much data is written to memory, potentially overwriting control data.

breakdown.explanation: A buffer gets more data than it can hold.

course.why: Memory corruption can crash software or redirect execution.
course.check_q: Which attack writes beyond buffer boundaries?

slides.title: Replay
slides.teach: A valid transmission or message is captured and resent later.

course.learn: A valid transmission or message is captured and resent later.

breakdown.explanation: Capture a valid message, then resend it.

course.why: Systems without replay protection may accept reused messages.
course.example: A previously valid authentication exchange is retransmitted.
course.check_q: Which attack resends a valid captured transmission?

slides.title: Privilege Escalation
slides.teach: An attacker gains permissions beyond those originally granted.

course.learn: An attacker gains permissions beyond those originally granted.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker gets more access than they should have.
User to admin, Local privilege escalation

course.example: A standard user exploits a flaw and becomes administrator.

slides.title: Directory Traversal
slides.teach: An attacker manipulates file paths to access files outside the intended directory.

course.learn: An attacker manipulates file paths to access files outside the intended directory.

breakdown.explanation: Escape the allowed folder using path manipulation.

course.why: Poor path validation can expose sensitive files.
course.example: ../../etc/passwd is requested through a web application.
course.check_q: Which attack uses path manipulation such as ../?

blocks.title: Network and Application Attacks comparison
rows: Third parties send replies to victim

blocks.title: Read the traffic behavior
items: Many systems flood one target → DDoS
The attack is distributed across multiple sources.
Example: Thousands of bots overwhelm a website.
Tiny requests cause huge responses → AMPLIFIED
Responses are much larger than requests.
Example: Small DNS queries generate large responses.
Third parties reply to victim → REFLECTED
Example: DNS servers send responses to a victim that never queried them.
Example: Login traffic is captured between user and server.
Previously captured auth material is reused.
Example: A stolen token is replayed.
Paths are manipulated to leave the intended directory.
blocks.example: Memory: Many = DDoS · Bigger reply = amplified · Others reply = reflected · Middle = on-path · Reuse = replay.

questions.q: Thousands of compromised hosts flood one website until it becomes unavailable. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: A DDoS uses many distributed sources to overwhelm one target.

questions.q: Small DNS queries trigger much larger responses toward a victim. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Amplification uses protocols whose responses are much larger than requests.

questions.q: Attackers spoof the victim's IP so third-party DNS servers send replies to the victim. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Reflection causes third parties to send responses to the spoofed victim address.

questions.q: A legitimate domain resolves to an attacker-controlled IP because name resolution was manipulated. Which category best fits?
An attacker intercepts and modifies traffic between a user and server. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: An on-path attacker sits between communicating parties.

questions.q: A stolen authentication token is reused successfully. Which attack best fits?
questions.explanation: Previously captured authentication material is being reused.

questions.q: A form field is interpreted as part of a backend command. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: Injection occurs when untrusted input becomes commands or code.

questions.q: A standard user exploits a flaw and becomes an administrator. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: The attacker gains higher privileges than originally granted.

questions.q: A request includes ../../ to access files outside the intended folder. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: Directory traversal escapes the intended path using manipulated file paths.
